title: Design a notification service
dek: Zotato sends login OTPs, "your order is on the way" updates and a Diwali offer to 5 crore people, by push, SMS and email. Build one service that sends them all, where an OTP is never stuck behind a promotion and nobody gets the same message twice.

items: Other services don't talk to SMS or push providers themselves. They send one event (who, which template, how urgent) to a notification service, which does the rest.
Keep separate lanes by priority: urgent (OTPs), normal (order updates), bulk (promotions). Workers always empty the urgent lane first, so a promotion to crores never delays an OTP.
Check preferences before sending: opted out, quiet hours, how many promotions this week, which devices and language.
Every event carries an id, so a retried request sends once. Newer order updates replace older ones that haven't gone out yet.
Providers fail. Retry with backoff, switch SMS to a second provider, drop push tokens the provider says are dead, and record what happened to every message.
Send by push, SMS and email, from one API, using templates in several languages.
Three kinds of message: OTPs (seconds matter), order updates (within a few seconds), promotions (within the hour is fine).
Respect each person's choices: opt-outs, quiet hours, a cap on promotions.
Know what happened to each message: sent, delivered, failed, and why.
Out of scope here: choosing who gets a campaign (the marketing team's tool), and in-app inboxes.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: OTPs out in under 2 seconds, order updates in under 5, even during a promotion
A retried request never sends the same message twice
One provider down doesn't stop OTPs
6 crore order updates and 20 lakh OTPs a day, plus promotions to 5 crore people at once

items: Order updates: 1 crore orders a day × about 6 updates each is 6 crore a day, about 700 a second on average and 2,000 at dinner.
OTPs: 20 lakh a day is about 23 a second. Tiny, but each one has a person waiting.
A Diwali promotion to 5 crore people. Sent over an hour, that's about 14,000 a second, seven times the dinner peak of order updates, all of it waiting in the bulk lane.
SMS costs money per message and providers limit how fast you may send; push is free but needs a valid token per device. Both shape the design.
Event: `id` (from the caller), `user_id`, `template`, `data`, `priority`, `collapse_key` (optional, e.g. the order id).
Preferences: per person, channels allowed, quiet hours, language, promotion cap.
Device: `user_id`, `push_token`, `platform`, `last_seen`.
Delivery: `event_id`, `channel`, `provider`, `status`, `attempts`, `error`.

body.label: API
body.say: Send one event and get its id back at once; the service picks channels and sends. Ask later what happened to it.

body.cap: Services send events to the notification API. It checks each person's preferences, then puts each message in the lane for its priority. Channel workers take urgent first and send through push, SMS and email providers.

body.x: The API answers as soon as the event is checked and queued. Everything slow (providers, retries) happens behind the lanes, so a slow SMS provider never slows the order service that asked for the message.
Lanes, so the OTP doesn't wait

body.name: First try
body.what: Every message goes on one queue, and workers send them in order.
body.use: Simple, and fine until the first big promotion.
body.avoid: At 8 pm marketing queues 5 crore Diwali messages. An OTP queued a second later waits behind all of them, and the customer can't log in for an hour.
body.ex: Ananya taps "Send OTP" three times during the Diwali blast. Three OTPs arrive 50 minutes later, all expired.
body.like: A single billing counter: you hold one bottle of water, and the person ahead is buying for a whole wedding.

body.name: Better
body.what: Separate queues for urgent, normal and bulk, each with its own workers or a strict rule that workers take urgent first. The bulk lane is drained at a set rate so it can't swamp providers.
body.use: OTPs and order updates go out in seconds whatever marketing is doing.
body.avoid: The bulk lane can wait a long time; that's acceptable for promotions, and the rate is a setting, not an accident.
body.ex: The Diwali blast drains over an hour; Ananya's OTP goes into the empty urgent lane and arrives in 2 seconds.
body.like: An express counter for a few items, open no matter how long the main queue is.

body.cap: The bulk lane holds 5 crore promotions, drained over about an hour. An OTP arrives in the middle of it, goes into the empty urgent lane and is sent in about 2 seconds.

body.x: Never twice, and never out of date

items: The caller gives each event an id. If the order service retries after a timeout, the API sees the id, finds it already queued, and does nothing new.

Channel workers record each event and channel as they send, and skip any already marked sent. A crash between sending and recording can still send one duplicate; providers are at-least-once too, so we cut duplicates down rather than promise none. Push providers also take a collapse key and show only the newest message for it.
Order updates replace each other: if "rider assigned" is still waiting when "on the way" arrives with the same collapse key, send only "on the way". Nobody needs both.
Check opt-outs and quiet hours before queuing, so little waits in a lane only to be dropped. Bulk messages wait longer, so the bulk worker checks again just before sending.
Promotions don't go out late at night, and promotional SMS must follow India's rules (TRAI's DLT: registered sender ids and templates, and the national do-not-disturb list).
Cap promotions per person per week, so one person isn't hit by five campaigns in a day.
Pick channels in order: push first (free, instant); SMS only for what must reach someone without the app, like OTPs.
An SMS provider is slow or down: after a few failures, switch OTPs to a second provider. Keep two from the start.
A provider rejects a push token as no longer valid: delete it, so the next message isn't wasted on it.
Temporary errors: retry with growing waits and a little randomness. After a few tries, park the message for a look instead of retrying for ever.
The notification service itself is down: callers keep their events (an outbox on their side) and send them when it's back. OTPs are re-requested by the person anyway.
Junior / mid: one API in front of the providers, a queue, templates, preferences, retries.
Senior: priority lanes and the promotion numbers, ids against duplicates, collapse keys, quiet hours and opt-outs before queuing.
Lead: provider failover, rate limits from providers, delivery tracking and dead tokens, the rules for promotional SMS in India.
"Send at the best time for each person?" Store a send-after time with each bulk message; the bulk worker skips messages that aren't due.
"How do you know a push was read?" The app reports opens; providers only report delivery to the device, sometimes not even that.
"A template has a mistake and 10 lakh are queued?" A switch to pause a campaign's messages in the bulk lane, checked by workers before sending.
"Several devices?" Send push to each active device; collapse keys stop the same update stacking up on each.
"How do you test it?" Fake providers that fail, slow down and return bad tokens, then check that OTPs still meet their target during a promotion.

body.x: A promotion blast is a burst a queue can hold, if what's behind it drains at a steady rate. The Monday sync challenge is the same idea.

practice.brief: Each test sends notification requests. Each one checks the person's preferences and records the delivery: 2 queries. Sending to push, SMS and email can happen just after. Your Clients' own rate is ignored.

tests.name: A normal afternoon
tests.desc: 700 notifications a second: order updates and OTPs.

checks.label: Notifications are sent, and retried, by workers taking them from a queue

tests.name: The dinner peak
tests.desc: 2,000 a second for an hour from 8 pm, the dinner peak.

tests.name: The Diwali promotion
tests.desc: At 8 pm marketing sends a promotion to 5 crore people: 14,000 notifications a second for 15 minutes, on top of dinner. OTPs still have to go out.

checks.label: Promotions wait in a queue (the bulk lane)

tests.name: A server group dies
tests.desc: At the peak (2,000 a second) the busiest group of servers crashes; it is back 5 minutes later.

checks.label: At least 99.5% of notifications still succeed
No server group that every request depends on (no single point of failure)

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the busiest database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

checks.label: At least 99.8% of notifications still succeed
Every database has a standby in another zone (Multi-AZ)

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (700 a second). Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails, like a memory limit.

tests.name: Send an OTP
tests.desc: An OTP by SMS for u1; the delivery workers send it.

fr.label: Send by push, SMS and email from one API
Priorities: OTPs first, promotions can wait
Respect opt-outs, quiet hours and caps

est.label: Order updates a second at dinner
Promotion rate (5 crore in an hour)

decisions.q: The SMS provider is down for 10 minutes. What happens?
options: The send fails, and the calling service has to retry it later
Retry with growing gaps, then switch to a second provider
Send the same message by email instead, straight away
decisions.why: Outside providers do fail. The queue holds the messages, retries space out, and a second provider keeps OTPs flowing. Pushing retries onto every caller spreads the problem; an email OTP arrives where nobody is looking.

decisions.q: A retry might send the same OTP twice. How do you stop that?
options: Never retry a send that might have gone through
Wait a minute before every retry, so the first can finish
Each notification has an id; senders skip ids already sent
decisions.why: Retries are needed, so sending must be safe to repeat: an id makes the second attempt a no-op. Never retrying loses messages, and waiting only makes duplicates rarer, not impossible.

decisions.q: A Diwali promotion to 5 crore people and login OTPs go out together. Which first?
options: Separate queues: OTPs and order updates first
One queue, first come first served
One queue, with OTPs sent by a second worker pool
decisions.why: An OTP stuck behind 5 crore promotions is useless. Separate queues keep urgent messages moving whatever the backlog; a second worker pool on one queue still has to wait behind the promotion.

hints.x: An OTP with a person waiting and a promotion to 5 crore people go through the same service. How do you keep one from delaying the other?
Order updates, OTPs and a promotion: three very different rates. The promotion is 7× dinner.
One POST with a caller-made id (so a retry doesn't send twice), a template and a priority; it returns 202. A GET shows what happened.
Accept fast, send later: a Queue between the API servers and the sending workers.
Workers sized for a steady rate drain the promotion over the following minutes; the queue holds it meanwhile.
Two groups of API servers and workers, a Multi-AZ database for the delivery records.

wrong.name: One server group
wrong.why: When it crashes, nothing answers for 5 minutes.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: A crash keeps it down for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: No queue
wrong.why: The burst hits the database directly and crashes it.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: Passes the load but costs far more than the traffic needs.

wrong.name: Right sizes, general parts
wrong.why: The sizes and redundancy are right, but no component does the job this problem turns on, so the design would carry the traffic without doing what was asked.

wrong.name: Notifications without a channel
wrong.why: Nothing records whether a message goes by SMS, push or email.
